conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You’re here because of nausea and vomiting that started this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up vomiting and did it seven times before coming in. I haven’t been able to keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of gastroparesis from your Type 1 diabetes, correct? And a gastric pacer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pacer was adjusted just a week ago. I was doing so well—no vomiting at all—until today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s frustrating. We’ll need to figure out why this came back. Any fever, pain, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or pain. Just the vomiting. And I haven’t changed my diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good to know. We’ve started IV fluids and anti-nausea meds—Zofran and Reglan. Your blood sugar was high at 256, so we’re watching that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I couldn’t take my insulin this morning because I was vomiting. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving insulin through the IV to keep it under control. Once you can eat again, we’ll restart your usual glargine at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I was really scared when my oxygen dropped in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was likely from the Ativan—sometimes it can make breathing shallow, especially when you're drowsy from vomiting. Your oxygen is back to normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense. So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray to check for a blockage. It didn’t show any obstruction, which is good. Your pacer is still in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s probably my gastroparesis acting up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. But we also want to check your esophagus and stomach directly. We’re planning an endoscopy in the next day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like a scope down my throat? Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel it. We’ll look for any inflammation or tight spots. Last time, you had a Botox injection to relax the pylorus—that helped, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it worked great for months. Could I get that again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll see what we find. We may also take a small tissue sample to check for infection or irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. My blood pressure has been high lately too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been elevated—188 over 86 on admission. Since you’re not on any blood pressure meds, we’re starting you on lisinopril tomorrow if it stays high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my kidneys? I’ve had kidney issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is normal at 0.8, so your kidneys are doing well. We’ll monitor it. Lisinopril can actually protect your kidneys long-term with diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good to know. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative—no infection in the blood. Urine culture was contaminated, so not reliable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no UTI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. No fever or symptoms to suggest it. Your white count is normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood sugar? It’s been hard to manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted endocrinology. Once you start eating, your sugars may rise temporarily. We’ll adjust your insulin then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still not hungry. Just the thought of food makes me nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving anti-nausea meds. The endoscopy is scheduled for tomorrow morning. That may help relieve the blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the endoscopy. You did great. We found white patches in your esophagus—signs of a fungal infection called candidiasis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fungal infection? But I feel fine otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common in people with diabetes. We took biopsies, but they didn’t show fungus—still, we’re treating it because the scope findings are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do we treat it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With an antifungal pill—fluconazole. One dose today, then one daily for six days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Did you do the Botox injection too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we injected Botox into your pylorus in five spots. It should help the stomach empty better. That’s often why people with gastroparesis vomit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope it works again. What about the inflammation you mentioned last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsies showed inflammation in your esophagus and stomach—gastritis. We’re starting a stronger acid blocker, pantoprazole, twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on something for that before. This is stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice daily should help reduce irritation and possibly the nausea too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you kept down some apple juice and crackers last night. That’s a big step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was so nervous, but it stayed down. Can I eat more today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance you to a soft diet—things like mashed potatoes, oatmeal. Small, frequent meals are best with gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I took my glargine last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we restarted your glargine. Your fasting sugar this morning was 144—excellent. Keep using your humalog as needed with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. My blood pressure has been better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, on lisinopril, it’s been in the 140s over 80s. Much improved. We’ll keep you on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full meals and no vomiting. We think you’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s wonderful. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding three: fluconazole for the fungal infection, lisinopril for blood pressure, and pantoprazole twice a day for stomach inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Zofran for nausea if it comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take it as needed. But be careful—Zofran can cause constipation. Use senna and docusate if you don’t have a bowel movement in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, see your gastroenterologist in two weeks. They’ll review the biopsy results and check your progress. Also follow up with endocrinology for your diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I was really worried this would never get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come a long way. The Botox and treatment for the infection should help. Keep up with small meals and your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. You’re alert, eating well, and your labs are stable. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I can’t wait. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call us if you start vomiting again, can’t keep fluids down, or have high fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll make those follow-up appointments today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and I hope you stay symptom-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home. We’re glad we could help.
